name: Camera field of view
seoDesc: Camera field of view: work out focal length (f) from the distance and the sensor size. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Camera field of view calculator the distance and the sensor size and it returns focal length (f). Think of it as a shortcut for whatever you happen to be working on. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Camera field of view calculator work?
sections.html:
The Camera field of view calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports focal length (f) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the distance, the sensor size (width) and the sensor size (diagonal).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Camera field of view calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Focal length (f)=(1 ÷ 2) × (sensor size (width)) ÷ the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × angle of view (horizontal))
Focal length (f)=(1 ÷ 2) × (sensor size (height)) ÷ the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × angle of view (vertical))
Focal length (f)=(1 ÷ 2) × (sensor size (diagonal)) ÷ the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × angle of view (diagonal))
Field of view (horizontal)=2 × distance × the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × angle of view (horizontal))
Field of view (vertical)=2 × distance × the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × angle of view (vertical))
Field of view (diagonal)=2 × distance × the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × angle of view (diagonal))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Sensor size (width) = 30 mm and Angle of view (horizontal) = 10 deg. Working through the relationship above gives Focal length (f) = 171.4508 mm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Focal length (f) = 171.4508 mm should be roughly the size you expected from Sensor size (width) = 30 mm and Angle of view (horizontal) = 10 deg.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Camera field of view calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the distance and the sensor size — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Camera field of view calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns focal length (f), derived from the distance and the sensor size. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Camera field of view calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the distance and the sensor size, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter focal length (f) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Focal length (f) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Focal length (f) = 171.4508 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Camera field of view calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
